newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition wins Belgrade, claims fraud elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: Opposition wins Belgrade, claims fraud elsewhere.

text.p: The opposition Zajedno coalition has wrested control over the Serbian capital of Belgrade in municipal elections, dealing a stunning blow to the ruling Socialists of President Slobodan Milosevic.

"Zajedno won 60 seats, the Socialist Party of Serbia 23, the Serbian Radical Party 15 and the Serbian Democratic Party won two," Belgrade election commission chairman Dragoslav Lazarevic told reporters on Tuesday.
But tensions were rising across Serbia as thousands of opposition supporters protested against what they called massive fraud in results from Sunday's elections, engineered to deny them victory.
Lazarevic said that in Belgrade voting would be repeated for 10 counsellors next Sunday. The city assembly has 110 seats.
Several thousand people celebrated in the city's central square, many with tears in their eyes.
"Oh God, I have never thought I would see the day when communism goes down," said an elderly Belgrader.

But the authorities were putting up a bitter fight in the Serbian industrial town of Nis, where thousands were protesting the city's commission decision to annul results from as many as 19 polling stations.
Opposition leaders have promised not to budge from the city hall until the commission revokes its decision.

Vuk Draskovic, head of the Serbian Renewal Movement, also part of the Zajedno coalition, told his supporters in Nis to defend their victory by any means and warned the authorities not to tamper with the results.
In 1991, he led protests against state control of the media which Milosevic crushed with tanks after two men were killed.
Results were also cancelled in the towns of Smederevska Palanka, Jagodina, Pancevo and Uzice. Residents of some those towns took to central squares to voice protest.
The opposition also claimed victory in Kragujevac, Uzice, Kraljevo, Kikinda, Zrenjanin and Cacak, and in Novi Sad, the provincial capital of Vojvodina.
Opposition supporters joked that Milosevic would have to shift his capital from Belgrade now that it is ruled by his foes.

"The SPS throughout Serbia is trying to annul election results by falsifying election records and lodging complaints," the Democratic Party, one of the Zajedno allies, said in a statement faxed to Reuters.
"The Socialists simply cannot admit their defeat and are trying to provoke disturbances and demonstrations throughout the country," the Democratic Party said.
Tensions were also rising in Kraljevo where protest could turn into riots, Ljiljana Radonjic, a Democratic Party spokeswoman in the central Serbian town, told Reuters.
Opposition leaders on hunger strike inside the city hall building are receiving a flood of offers for assistance from surrounding towns, she said.
The scale of the defeat apparently stunned Milosevic's Socialist Party (SPS), who were lulled by their victory at federal elections two weeks ago.
The Socialist coalition claimed to have captured 134 out of 174 municipalities in Serbia.

But the loss of the major cities, where industrial unrest against poverty and joblessness has recently increased, would be a severe blow to the Socialists' prestige ahead of Serbian parliamentary elections scheduled for next year.
Analysts said voters appeared to have voted one way in the federal elections to keep Milosevic in power and another in the municipal poll to rein in his Socialists.

Yugoslav voters have been reluctant to trust the opposition, preferring to stay with Milosevic who wields complete control over the press, army, police and national administration as well as the country's purse strings.
Political sources said the Socialist-led government had more than enough power to frustrate opposition-controlled municipal councils and make them look inept.
